You don't get bogged down in overthinking or analysis paralysis; you read the situation, trust your experiential pattern-recognition, and move forward with steady confidence. You keep daily operations flowing smoothly. The risk is that relying on unexamined instinct for novel, counter-intuitive strategic problems can lead to costly cognitive biases that data would have easily exposed. Your viewpoint is that 80% of daily choices are not rocket science, and that trusting your gut saves invaluable time.
decision-making-style.pragmatic_arbitrator: You embody the balanced ideal of decision-making, skillfully blending data analysis with intuitive wisdom and practical common sense. You gather key metrics to understand the landscape, check in with your gut instincts regarding the human factors, and decide with confidence when you reach 70% certainty, adjusting course as reality unfolds. The critique is that this balanced middle ground can satisfy no one completely—appearing too slow for impulsive gamblers and too reckless for academic purists. Your conviction is that real-world leadership requires both head and heart, and that adaptable judgment beats rigid dogma.
decision-making-style.data_driven_commander: You demand hard metrics, empirical evidence, and clear statistical indicators fast, using them to make bold, rapid strategic decisions under high pressure. You strip emotion and sentimentality out of the boardroom, focusing strictly on what the numbers demonstrate and executing with decisive authority. You outpace slower rivals through analytical velocity. The shadow side is that numbers can be manipulated to fit preconceived biases, and ignoring human morale and ethical intuition can lead to disastrous cultural revolts. Your response is that feelings lie while numbers don't, and that fast, evidence-based execution is what wins.
decision-making-style.gut_initiator: You leap into high-stakes action based on instantaneous gut conviction, creative vision, and bold hunches. You believe that momentum is the greatest teacher, preferring to make a call in five seconds, launch into the arena, and learn through direct trial and error rather than wasting weeks in theoretical debates. The critique is that impulsive leaps can lead to reckless mistakes, wasted resources, and sudden reversals that leave your team exhausted and whiplashed. Your defense is that you cannot learn to swim by reading books in a library, and that those who hesitate are forever trapped on the shore.
decision-making-style.swift_pragmatist: You prioritize rapid forward momentum and bias-for-action over agonizing analysis. You believe that a good decision made today is infinitely superior to a perfect decision made next month, trusting your ability to course-correct in real time based on live market feedback. You test hypotheses through direct action. The limitation is that moving too fast can cause you to skip crucial due diligence, signing contracts or entering partnerships that create legal, structural, or ethical headaches later. Your perspective is that in a fast-moving world, speed is defense, and that the only unforgivable error is stagnation.
decision-making-style.calculated_disruptor: You combine sharp, rigorous analytical insights with lightning-fast, decisive execution to outmaneuver competitors and seize sudden openings. You identify the decisive metric or structural weakness in a system, calculate the asymmetric risk-reward ratio, and strike with total commitment before others have even finished their preliminary research. The danger is that your high-velocity, calculated aggression can create intense friction with stakeholders and alienate partners who feel outpaced or steamrolled. Your conviction is that history belongs to those who see the future clearly and have the courage to act on it without blinking.

about.title: About
about.lede: Standpointly places you on two independent axes and names the region you land in. It is a self-report instrument, which means it measures what you say about yourself on a particular afternoon — useful, but not the same as measuring what you would do.
about.s1_body: The horizontal axis runs from collective provision to private enterprise: who should own things, and who should decide how they are distributed. The vertical axis runs from personal liberty to social authority: how much the state may direct private conduct. They are deliberately independent, because in practice they are — economic and social views come apart in people far more often than a single left-to-right line allows.
about.s2_title: Why a grid and not a compass
about.s2_body: An earlier version placed people on a compass rose with eight bearings. It looked better and read worse: a bearing tells you a direction but not a magnitude, and readers consistently mistook the needle for a verdict. A 3×3 grid can be taught in one animation — the vertical guide finds your economic score, the horizontal finds your social one, and the cell where they cross is the name you get. The precision standpoint mark survives as the logo.
about.s3_body: It is not a diagnosis, not a prediction of how you vote, and not a measure of how well-informed you are. Nine named regions cannot contain the actual variety of political belief, and the name you get is a label for a neighbourhood, not a description of you. If a statement felt like it was missing an option you would have chosen, that is a real limitation of the format and not a subtle test of something.
about.s4_body: Every statement, weight, region name and illustration here is original work. None of it is derived from other published political tests, whose propositions are copyrighted and whose weights were never disclosed in any case.

method.title: Method
method.lede: Everything below is what the code actually does. The numbers on this page are read from the live test configuration rather than typed here, so they cannot drift out of date.
method.s1_body: {questions} statements, each answered on a five-point scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree. {xCount} load on the {xAxis} axis alone, {yCount} on the {yAxis} axis alone, and {crossCount} load on both at once. Each statement carries a signed weight per axis; a negative weight means agreement moves you toward the negative pole.
method.s2_body: Your answers map to −2…+2. For each axis the raw score is the sum of your answer multiplied by that statement's weight for the axis. The raw score is divided by the axis maximum ({xMax} for {xAxis}, {yMax} for {yAxis}), multiplied by a gain of {gain}, and clamped to ±{clamp}. The gain exists because dividing by the theoretical maximum alone pins almost everyone near the origin — nobody answers every question at the extreme.
method.s3_title: Why agreeing with everything puts you in the centre
method.s3_body: The weights on each axis sum to exactly zero. Someone who agrees with all {questions} statements scores zero on both axes and lands in the middle cell. This is deliberate: acquiescence bias — the tendency to agree with whatever is put in front of you — is one of the best-documented artefacts in survey research, and an unbalanced instrument silently converts it into a political opinion. A continuous integration check fails the build if any weight edit breaks the balance.
method.s4_body: Each axis is divided at ±{band}. Below the lower boundary is the first column or row, above the upper boundary is the third, and anything between is the middle. That produces nine regions. The boundaries are a presentational choice rather than a discovered threshold: someone at {bandJustUnder} and someone at {bandJustOver} are described differently while being, in truth, nearly identical.
method.s5_body: The gain of {gain} was calibrated against simulated respondents, not real ones. Simulated answer patterns spread wider than human ones, so the value is likely to need raising once a real sample exists. Until that pilot is run, treat the magnitude of your score as indicative and the cell you land in as approximate — particularly if you are close to a boundary.
method.s6_body: There are none on the grid, and there will be none until each placement has a stated method and a citable source published here. Plotting well-known figures from impression alone would be inventing data and presenting it as measurement.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.lede: Standpointly is built with privacy by design: your test answers are processed locally in your browser and are never stored in a user database.
privacy.s1_body: Answers are held temporarily in your browser's sessionStorage while you take an assessment so a page refresh does not lose your progress. They are immediately cleared when the test finishes. Your individual answers are never uploaded or retained in a personal database.
privacy.s2_body: Scoring runs entirely in your browser using deterministic algorithms. The result is calculated as numerical coordinates encoded directly in the URL link. Standpointly does not maintain user accounts or personal profiles. Anyone with whom you choose to share your result link can view the plotted coordinates.

home.hero_title: Understand yourself. Understand the people around you.
home.hero_body: Standpointly builds measuring instruments, not quizzes. Each test asks you to react to a set of statements, scores them on two independent axes, and shows you where you land — with every weight and every formula published, so you can check the result instead of just believing it.
home.tests_body: Standpointly instruments are organized into 5 scientific fields. Discover where you stand across personality, relationships, beliefs, values, wellbeing, and work.
home.how_1_body: One statement per screen, five options, no time limit. There is no right answer and no trick question — a statement you find easy to agree with is doing exactly as much work as one you don't.
home.how_2_body: Each statement carries a weight on one or both axes. Your answers are summed, normalised, and placed on a grid. Because the weights on each axis cancel to zero, agreeing with everything puts you in the middle rather than anywhere flattering.
home.how_3_body: You get two numbers, a named region, and a description that includes the strongest objection to the position you landed in. The result lives in its own link, so you can keep it, share it, or throw it away.
home.why_1_body: Every formula, every constant and every known limitation is on the method page — including the fact that the current calibration is provisional until real pilot data exists.
home.why_2_body: No account, no database, no analytics, no cookies. Your answers stay in your browser and your result exists only in the URL you were given.
home.why_3_body: Nine named regions cannot contain the real variety of political belief, and the name you get is a label for a neighbourhood rather than a description of you. The site says so on the result page too.
